name: Freya Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government; we sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal working day involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Freya, 43. I earned a bachelor’s in music, and after years of work I accompany a local choir, record piano rehearsal tracks and teach children at the community hall. I know how to keep a shaky group together; I’m an ordinary player, not a concert soloist. I like hearing the choir find one ending, and I dislike chasing three small fees for one rehearsal.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is the household counting on from those fees?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner drives deliveries, with hours that change each week. We have two children in school, a mortgage and less than one month of expenses saved. My music pay is on the lower side, and there are few similar posts close enough to keep our school pickup routine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the choir that a tidy email list is fine, but somebody still has to follow a singer who comes in late. I expect our regular Wednesday rehearsal and my pupils to carry on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My problem is already the mortgage, not a new machine. A missed choir night and a short delivery week would empty what little we have in the account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep the Wednesday choir and five weekly pupils this winter. I would ask the choir treasurer for next month’s paid dates in writing, and if a rehearsal is cancelled I’d stop the paid practice-room booking before it renews.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious even with a mild story. A week without a fee shows up on the grocery list before anyone calls it a crisis.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill would a cancelled choir night touch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The electricity payment is the first one I would move, but moving it costs us later. I would phone the provider before it is overdue rather than hide the letter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use AI for a rehearsal track?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have never used an AI tool and do not want to put a child’s singing into one. I can play a rehearsal line and stop when the choir needs me to.

do: Keep the **Wednesday choir** and five pupils this winter.

feel: I feel **anxious** because even a mild scenario leaves our grocery budget fragile.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say quick rehearsal tracks and lesson plans could replace some small paid jobs. I’d ask our musicians’ union to put the rehearsal fee and recording reuse terms on one page.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The choir may keep me for live evenings but stop paying for practice recordings. Those tracks help cover our food bill, and my partner’s delivery hours cannot reliably fill the gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I’d list which choir dates are paid and ask the union for a shared recording clause. In the first year, if track orders fall, I’d cancel the separate practice room at renewal and ask the community hall for an extra paid adult choir hour only if it provides space and six adults prepay enough to cover my time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be alarmed because that small recording money is already in our food plan. I know how to teach a live group, but a room without paying people would leave us worse off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is the first paid task to go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first loss would be a piano track I make for singers to practise at home. Three piano rehearsal tracks cover a week of groceries.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could the players do together?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The union could ask every choir for written consent before recorded voices are reused and a minimum rehearsal fee. I cannot make that rule alone when another pianist needs the next booking.

I would ask the **musicians’ union** for fees and recording consent in writing.
think: Recorded **practice tracks** currently help cover our weekly food bill.
Variable **delivery pay** cannot reliably replace those small fees month after month.
do: List **paid choir dates** and ask the union for a recording clause this month.
Cancel **practice-room rent** at renewal in first year if track orders fall.
Offer an **adult choir hour** only if hall space is provided and six adults prepay enough for my time.
feel: I feel **alarmed** because lost track fees would hit food money.

fieldNote: The vulnerable **track fees** are small individually but already fund basic food.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the choir that thinking AGI by 2028 could make our tracks and plans cheaply, while robots that play hands-on parts arrive around 2031. Our live Wednesday fee might last longer, but I would not promise it to the mortgage lender.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The rehearsal tracks could disappear in 2028 and some parents might choose app lessons. If the choir also cuts a paid night, my partner’s delivery pay cannot cover food, school costs and the mortgage alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Before 2028 I’d ask the choir for written paid dates and list every bill with my partner. In the first year after AGI arrives, if tracks stop, I’d end the rented practice room at renewal, ask the lender for a temporary plan before missing a mortgage payment, and apply for a posted paid accompanist place only if the wage covers travel and school pickup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be alarmed and up at night. There are few places nearby for an ordinary accompanist, and less than a month’s savings does not buy a long audition tour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do before a missed mortgage payment?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would call the lender with the actual cancelled dates before the due date. A short payment plan might cost more overall, so I would ask for the total in writing before accepting it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Can you take another job without changing school pickup?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the five current pupils until another job sends a written offer. A new venue would need to finish early enough for pickup or pay enough for confirmed childcare.

I would tell the choir that a longer **live fee** is not guaranteed.
think: Practice tracks and some **pupil lessons** could end quickly.
Delivery wages alone cannot cover **mortgage** payments, food and school costs.
do: Keep **five pupils** until a written offer; end practice-room rent at renewal if track fees stop after 2028.
Ask the **lender** before a missed payment; require full extra interest and fees in writing before accepting a plan.
Seek **posted accompanist work** after 2028 only if tracks stop and pay covers travel and pickup or confirmed childcare.
feel: I feel **alarmed** about a likely loss with almost no savings or nearby options.
S2.quote: Our live Wednesday fee might last longer, but I would not promise it to the mortgage lender.
fieldNote: She expects **2028 thinking work** to go before 2031 robot hands could replace live playing.
Her **lender call** precedes missed payment; any new job needs posted pay and workable school pickup.

steps.text: Keep five pupils until written job offer; confirm paid choir dates and bills before 2028

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say five years is time to prove that live choir teaching earns its room, not a reason to stop playing now. Thinking AGI arrives around 2031 and capable playing robots follow around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might replace recording fees with adult coaching if enough people attend. I cannot pay a deposit on hall space from the mortgage account to find out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next term I’d ask the independent parish hall for a six-week adult singing group, but only if it gives me a room without a deposit and seven adults prepay enough for my time and confirmed childcare. In the first year after 2031, I’d repeat it only if seven still pay and my partner’s delivery rota leaves pickup covered; I’d keep the Wednesday choir while it pays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d still feel anxious about the bills we have today. The extra years let me test one group. No calendar date feeds the children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would five years let you arrange with the choir?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the treasurer to publish the rehearsal rate each season and give us notice before recordings are replaced. A written rate makes it easier to say no to unpaid preparation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would stop the new evening class from losing money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seven prepaid places would cover my time and a sitter if my partner cannot collect the children. If the hall asks for a deposit or only five pay, I would cancel the class before any family loses money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell my children that music is work when a person is paid for it, and that they can love it without owing it their whole life. Thinking AGI in 2036 and robot players around 2039 are separate dates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 I might still be accompanying the choir, but there is no pension hiding in a short rehearsal fee. The mortgage and thin savings are here in 2026, and a decade of warning does not pay them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I’d keep the choir and five pupils and put any cleared extra track fee toward the electricity arrears. Across the decade I’d build the adult group only with a free room, seven prepayments covering my time and childcare; in the first year after 2036 I’d keep the group only while it pays and seek a posted accompanist job if the choir drops my fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious about household money even with ten years to plan. If we build a small cushion, I might breathe more easily, but I cannot promise that from this winter’s work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you build before 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would start with the electricity balance, then one mortgage payment in reserve if extra fees arrive. I would not write a savings number on the fridge before money is in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you talk to the children about music work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the children to finish school and ask what a job pays. They can keep singing even if the paid work changes.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because track fees could vanish before I can replace grocery money, and a live night might also be cut. A written choir schedule, a short lender plan before arrears and a real accompanist vacancy with pay that covers pickup would help. I cannot turn a spare room into a wage without prepaid singers.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who pays for the rehearsal track a choir uses all week. The choir hears me on Wednesday, but the groceries come from the little tracks made on Thursday.

headlineQuote: The choir hears me on Wednesday, but the groceries come from the little tracks made on Thursday.
portrait: Freya is a **43-year-old accompanist** with a music bachelor’s, experienced in choir rehearsals, children’s lessons and piano tracks.
Her **lower pay**, variable delivery income, two children and mortgage leave less than a month saved.
She **never uses AI** and keeps written fees, paid choir work and union recording terms central to her plan.
Fast AGI threatens **practice tracks** before robot players arrive, so she tests a separately paid adult group only with prepayments.
biggestWorry: She fears **AGI by 2028** could erase grocery money from tracks before new paid work is ready.
whatWouldHelp: Written **choir dates** and a lender plan before arrears would buy time.
A posted **accompanist vacancy** covering travel and school pickup would let her seek replacement pay.
